strategies.title: Words in context
strategies.method: Read the surrounding idea and restate the missing meaning in everyday language. Then test each option in the sentence.
strategies.shortcut: Use contrast and cause clues to predict the meaning before the choices distract you.
strategies.caution: A familiar definition can be wrong in this context. Keep negation and tone intact.
strategies.example: Original example: “Although costly, the repair was essential” requires a word meaning necessary, not inexpensive.

strategies.title: Central idea and scope
strategies.method: State the topic and the main thing the author says about it. Check the beginning, turning point and ending.
strategies.shortcut: Reduce the passage to one sentence; compare every answer with that sentence.
strategies.caution: A true detail is not necessarily the main point. Avoid answers broader than the evidence.
strategies.example: Original example: a passage about one city testing buses does not establish that every city has solved pollution.

strategies.title: Text evidence and details
strategies.method: Locate the claim in the question, then find the exact passage evidence that supports it.
strategies.shortcut: Give every surviving choice an evidence location. Eliminate a choice with one unsupported required claim.
strategies.caution: Matching a word is not enough; the relationship and speaker must also match.
strategies.example: Original example: evidence that a device is cheaper does not show that it is more durable.

strategies.title: Inference and logical completion
strategies.method: Combine the stated facts into the smallest conclusion they support. Check each qualifier in the answer.
strategies.shortcut: Look for the missing logical link, then reject choices that need an extra assumption.
strategies.caution: Strong language can be correct when supported. Do not automatically reject all words such as always.
strategies.example: Original example: “All samples in this trial changed color” does not mean every possible sample will change color.

strategies.title: Sentence function and text structure
strategies.method: Describe what each relevant sentence does: introduces, exemplifies, challenges, explains or qualifies.
strategies.shortcut: Summarize the movement as two verbs, such as presents a claim → questions it.
strategies.caution: The subject of a sentence and its job in the argument are different things.
strategies.example: Original example: a laboratory result after a prediction may test the prediction, not introduce a new topic.

strategies.title: Paired texts and viewpoints
strategies.method: Summarize each author’s position separately. Find the precise issue on which the question asks you to compare them.
strategies.shortcut: Use a tiny A/B comparison: claim, evidence, agreement, disagreement.
strategies.caution: Do not transfer a statement from one author to the other. Shared subject does not imply shared opinion.
strategies.example: Original example: both authors can favor public transit while disagreeing about how to fund it.

strategies.title: Graphs supporting a text claim
strategies.method: Read the claim first, then the graph title, axes, units and legend. Identify which comparison would support the claim.
strategies.shortcut: Inspect only the relevant series once you understand the display.
strategies.caution: A statement can be numerically true but irrelevant. Correlation alone does not establish a cause.
strategies.example: Original example: a claim about faster growth needs a change over time, not just the largest final value.

strategies.title: Sentence boundaries
strategies.method: Identify subjects and finite verbs, and decide which groups are independent clauses before choosing punctuation.
strategies.shortcut: Two independent clauses can be joined by a semicolon, or by a comma plus a coordinating conjunction.
strategies.caution: A comma alone does not join independent clauses. A colon needs a complete clause before it.
strategies.example: Original example: “The trial ended; the researchers packed up.” Each side can stand alone.

strategies.title: Nonessential phrases and paired punctuation
strategies.method: Temporarily remove the inserted phrase and check the remaining sentence. Decide whether the phrase is essential to identifying its noun.
strategies.shortcut: A removable mid-sentence aside often needs matching punctuation at both ends.
strategies.caution: Do not insert commas around essential information or between a subject and its main verb.
strategies.example: Original example: “Our tutor, a former engineer, explains the model.” Removing the aside leaves a complete sentence.

strategies.title: Subject–verb agreement
strategies.method: Find the grammatical subject and its main verb. Set intervening phrases aside, then decide singular or plural.
strategies.shortcut: Cross out an intervening “of…” phrase while checking agreement.
strategies.caution: The noun nearest the verb may not be its subject. A gerund phrase can function as a singular subject.
strategies.example: Original example: “The box of pencils is missing.” The box, not the pencils, controls the verb.

strategies.title: Pronouns, plurals and ownership
strategies.method: Identify the noun the pronoun refers to, its number, and whether the sentence needs possession or a contraction.
strategies.shortcut: Expand contractions mentally: it’s → it is; they’re → they are.
strategies.caution: An apostrophe does not form a normal plural. Make sure the antecedent is unambiguous.
strategies.example: Original example: “The club changed its schedule” uses possession; “it’s closed” means it is closed.

strategies.title: Verb tense and form
strategies.method: Use the passage timeline to decide the tense. Identify whether the sentence already has a main verb.
strategies.shortcut: Time markers such as before, since and by then often resolve tense more quickly than how an option sounds.
strategies.caution: A participle alone may create a fragment. Do not force all verbs into one tense when times differ.
strategies.example: Original example: “She had left before the guests arrived” distinguishes two past events.

strategies.title: Modifiers and parallel structure
strategies.method: Place a description beside what it describes. Compare the grammatical form of items in a list or comparison.
strategies.shortcut: After an opening participial phrase, check who performs that action.
strategies.caution: A sentence can be grammatical yet describe the wrong actor. Parallel form must preserve meaning.
strategies.example: Original example: “Carrying the books, Maya opened the door” identifies the carrier; “the door opened” would not.

strategies.title: Concision without lost meaning
strategies.method: Remove duplicated meaning and unnecessary filler while preserving the needed facts and grammatical structure.
strategies.shortcut: Compare the shortest choice first, then test whether anything essential vanished.
strategies.caution: Shortest is not automatically correct. Keep required distinctions, transitions and details.
strategies.example: Original example: “They returned back again” may become “They returned” if the context does not require repetition.

strategies.title: Logical transitions
strategies.method: Describe the relationship between the ideas: contrast, cause, example, addition or sequence. Then choose the connector.
strategies.shortcut: Predict the relationship before considering the transition words.
strategies.caution: A transition that fits the topic can still reverse the logic. Read across the sentence boundary.
strategies.example: Original example: a successful outcome after a failed prediction calls for contrast, not a connector implying confirmation.

strategies.title: SAT notes and rhetorical goals
strategies.method: Read the requested writing goal, then select only notes that help accomplish it. Check every factual claim in the choice.
strategies.shortcut: Turn the goal into a checklist: compare two things, introduce a person, or emphasize a difference.
strategies.caution: Using many notes is not the objective. Accurate information can still miss the requested audience or purpose.
strategies.example: Original example: to compare two bridges’ lengths, use both measurements rather than only their architects’ names.

strategies.title: ACT add/delete and writer’s goal
strategies.method: Decide what the proposed sentence contributes to the paragraph’s purpose. Evaluate the explanation as well as yes or no.
strategies.shortcut: Name its role: relevant support, distraction, repetition or needed context.
strategies.caution: A fact being interesting or true is insufficient. The reason in the answer must also fit.
strategies.example: Original example: a recipe’s history may distract from a paragraph explaining a single safety step.

strategies.title: ACT sentence and paragraph placement
strategies.method: Find what information the sentence assumes and what the next sentence needs. Track pronouns, transitions and chronology.
strategies.shortcut: Look for dependency words such as this discovery; place the sentence after the discovery has been introduced.
strategies.caution: Reading only the sentence before a proposed location can miss a broken connection after it.
strategies.example: Original example: introduce a new researcher before referring to that person as she.

strategies.title: ACT tone and precise wording
strategies.method: Match the passage’s level of formality and choose the word that expresses the intended action exactly.
strategies.shortcut: Separate style errors from grammar errors when the choices mainly change vocabulary.
strategies.caution: Formal does not mean elaborate. A word can sound impressive and still mean the wrong thing.
strategies.example: Original example: “The team investigated the result” may fit a research account better than “checked the weird thing out.”

strategies.title: Solve for the requested quantity
strategies.method: Write the exact quantity requested before calculating. Look for an equation manipulation that produces it directly.
strategies.shortcut: If 4x + 9 = 29 and the task asks for 4x, subtract 9 without first finding x.
strategies.caution: Stop at the requested expression, not an intermediate answer. Check units and signs.
strategies.example: Original example: from 4x + 9 = 29, 4x = 20; x = 5 answers a different question.

strategies.title: Backsolve from numeric choices
strategies.method: Substitute a plausible answer into the original conditions and check whether all conditions hold.
strategies.shortcut: Ordered choices can speed the search when the relevant relationship is monotonic over the allowed domain.
strategies.caution: Starting in the middle only gives directional information under monotonicity. Quadratics and constraints can break that assumption.
strategies.example: Original example: for 3x + 4 = 25, test a candidate x in the original left side; keep one giving 25.

strategies.title: Choose values to eliminate expressions
strategies.method: For an identity-style question, choose permitted values and compare the original expression with each answer.
strategies.shortcut: Avoid 0 and 1 when they make distinct expressions accidentally equal; a second value can eliminate a tie.
strategies.caution: One matching example does not prove an identity. Respect restrictions and use algebra to resolve surviving choices.
strategies.example: Original example: x² and 2x agree at x = 2; checking x = 3 reveals they are different.

strategies.title: Estimate and eliminate impossible answers
strategies.method: Predict the sign, size and units before doing exact arithmetic. Remove choices outside a justified range.
strategies.shortcut: Wide spacing between answers can make an interval enough to identify the only possible choice.
strategies.caution: Close choices and student-produced answers usually need exact work. Sketches may not be drawn to scale.
strategies.example: Original example: 19% of 203 must be near 40, so 4 and 400 are unreasonable.

strategies.title: Units and rates
strategies.method: Write the units beside every factor and choose conversion fractions that cancel unwanted units.
strategies.shortcut: Let unit cancellation guide the setup before multiplying numbers.
strategies.caution: Converting square or cubic units requires squaring or cubing the conversion factor.
strategies.example: Original example: 3 hours × 60 minutes/hour = 180 minutes; square feet require area conversions.

strategies.title: Percent change and reverse percentages
strategies.method: Identify the base quantity. Convert each change to a multiplier and apply changes in order.
strategies.shortcut: A 15% increase is ×1.15; to recover the old amount, divide the new amount by 1.15.
strategies.caution: Equal percent increases and decreases do not cancel because their bases differ.
strategies.example: Original example: 100 × 1.20 × 0.80 = 96, not 100.

strategies.title: Ratios and proportional shares
strategies.method: Express the parts as multiples of a common unit. Use the total to find the size of that unit.
strategies.shortcut: Add ratio parts first, then divide the total by their sum.
strategies.caution: Part-to-part ratios are not part-to-whole fractions. Confirm whether the relationship is proportional.
strategies.example: Original example: splitting 70 in a 2:5 ratio gives seven units of 10, hence shares 20 and 50.

strategies.title: Systems and number of solutions
strategies.method: Align coefficients and use elimination or substitution. Before solving, inspect whether equations describe the same or parallel lines.
strategies.shortcut: Proportional variable coefficients with incompatible constants mean no solution.
strategies.caution: Proportional coefficients and constants mean infinitely many solutions, not none.
strategies.example: Original example: x + y = 3 and 2x + 2y = 8 are inconsistent; replacing 8 by 6 makes them the same line.

strategies.title: SAT graphing: intersections and intercepts
strategies.method: In the SAT testing calculator, graph each side as a function or graph both equations. Inspect intersections and verify in the original equation.
strategies.shortcut: An intersection can give a candidate solution; an x-intercept can locate a zero.
strategies.caution: Adjust the viewing window and check domain restrictions. An approximate graph does not prove an exact identity or show every root. Practice in Bluebook’s calculator.
strategies.example: Original example: graph y = 2x + 1 and y = 7 to find a candidate x, then substitute it back.

strategies.title: Quadratic roots and vertex
strategies.method: Choose the useful form: factored for zeros, vertex form for the turning point, expanded form for coefficients.
strategies.shortcut: For y = a(x − h)² + k, the vertex is (h,k); for y = (x − r)(x − s), zeros are r and s.
strategies.caution: Read signs carefully. The vertex is a minimum only if a is positive.
strategies.example: Original example: y = 2(x − 4)² + 3 has minimum value 3 at x = 4.

strategies.title: Quadratic number of real solutions
strategies.method: For ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0, compute b² − 4ac to count distinct real roots.
strategies.shortcut: Positive gives two, zero gives one repeated real root, negative gives no real roots.
strategies.caution: First put the equation in standard form. If a depends on a parameter, check separately when a becomes zero.
strategies.example: Original example: x² + 2x + 5 = 0 has discriminant −16, so it has no real roots.

strategies.title: Linear versus exponential change
strategies.method: Check whether equal steps add a constant amount or multiply by a constant factor. Build the corresponding model.
strategies.shortcut: A repeated percent change becomes the base of an exponential expression.
strategies.caution: The exponent must count matching time intervals. A changing percentage is not a fixed multiplier model.
strategies.example: Original example: 200 growing 3% per year is 200(1.03)^t after t years.

strategies.title: Function evaluation and transformations
strategies.method: Substitute the input with parentheses, then apply operations in order. For a transformation, track inside and outside changes separately.
strategies.shortcut: Build a tiny input/output table when notation is confusing.
strategies.caution: f(x + h) shifts a graph left by h; adding h outside shifts it up. Squaring a negative input needs parentheses.
strategies.example: Original example: if f(x) = x² − 1, then f(−3) = (−3)² − 1 = 8.

strategies.title: Rational and radical equations
strategies.method: Record denominator restrictions first. Isolate radicals before squaring, then check candidates in the original equation.
strategies.shortcut: Factoring may cancel common factors after you record excluded inputs.
strategies.caution: Squaring can introduce extraneous solutions; cancellation never restores an excluded input.
strategies.example: Original example: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) simplifies to x + 2 only when x ≠ 2.

strategies.title: Similar figures, area and volume
strategies.method: Identify the length scale factor between similar figures and the dimension of the requested quantity.
strategies.shortcut: Lengths scale by k, areas by k², volumes by k³.
strategies.caution: The figures must be similar. Equal area alone does not determine a common side scale.
strategies.example: Original example: doubling every length multiplies surface area by 4 and volume by 8.

strategies.title: Right triangles and trigonometric ratios
strategies.method: Mark the angle, opposite side, adjacent side and hypotenuse. Use the relevant ratio or the Pythagorean theorem.
strategies.shortcut: Recognize verified 3–4–5 or 5–12–13 side ratios to reduce arithmetic.
strategies.caution: The ratio depends on the marked angle. Check degree/radian mode and confirm a right angle.
strategies.example: Original example: for an angle opposite the 3-side in a 3–4–5 triangle, sine is 3/5 and cosine is 4/5.

strategies.title: Circle equations, arcs and sectors
strategies.method: Read center and radius from (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². Use the angle’s fraction of a full turn for an arc or sector.
strategies.shortcut: Arc length is θ/360 times the circumference when θ is in degrees.
strategies.caution: The right side of the circle equation is radius squared, not radius. Radian formulas require radians.
strategies.example: Original example: a 90° sector contains one quarter of the circle’s area.

strategies.title: Means, totals and spread
strategies.method: Convert a mean to a total using total = count × mean. For combined groups, add totals and counts separately.
strategies.shortcut: A missing observation equals the required total minus the known total.
strategies.caution: Averaging group means is valid only with equal group sizes. Spread and center describe different features.
strategies.example: Original example: two scores averaging 80 and three averaging 90 have mean (160 + 270)/5 = 86.

strategies.title: Probability and conditional sample spaces
strategies.method: Define the possible outcomes and the event. If a condition is given, restrict the sample space to that group first.
strategies.shortcut: In a two-way table, a “given” condition usually identifies the new denominator.
strategies.caution: Multiplying marginal probabilities requires independence. With no replacement, later denominators change.
strategies.example: Original example: among 12 selected club members, 3 play chess; within that group the proportion is 3/12.

strategies.title: Samples, experiments and claims
strategies.method: Ask how participants were selected and whether treatments were randomly assigned. Separate association from a causal claim.
strategies.shortcut: Selection concerns generalization; assignment concerns comparing treatment effects.
strategies.caution: Large samples do not repair systematic selection bias. A margin of error is not a guarantee that a particular interval contains the truth.
strategies.example: Original example: a voluntary online survey may overrepresent people with strong views even if many respond.

strategies.title: Science data lookup and comparisons
strategies.method: Read the question’s named table or figure, variables, units and legend. Locate the exact condition before comparing values.
strategies.shortcut: For a direct lookup, use the referenced display first, then read the context needed to interpret it.
strategies.caution: Do not generalize “never read the passage.” Definitions, methods and viewpoint questions require text.
strategies.example: Original example: comparing two habitats requires the same species, behavior and unit in both columns.

strategies.title: Science trends and predictions
strategies.method: Follow the requested series as one variable changes. Distinguish a measured point from an estimate between or beyond points.
strategies.shortcut: Sketch a small ↑, ↓ or flat note for each relevant relationship.
strategies.caution: A trend may change direction. Extrapolation needs an explicit assumption that the relationship continues.
strategies.example: Original example: increasing values from 10 to 20 do not establish the trend at 100.

strategies.title: Science experimental design
strategies.method: Identify what was varied, what was measured and what was held constant. Compare trials that isolate the variable in the question.
strategies.shortcut: Write a three-part note: changed / measured / controlled.
strategies.caution: Two changed factors can confound a comparison. Repeated trials improve reliability but do not automatically remove bias.
strategies.example: Original example: to test light’s effect on growth, keep water and plant type consistent across light conditions.

strategies.title: Science competing explanations
strategies.method: Summarize each explanation and the prediction it makes. Test the proposed observation against each prediction separately.
strategies.shortcut: Build a small support / contradict / does not distinguish table.
strategies.caution: A result can fit several explanations. Distinguish what a speaker claims from established fact.
strategies.example: Original example: two models may both predict melting, but disagree about whether warming occurs above or below the ice.

strategies.title: Science background knowledge
strategies.method: Use supplied definitions first; recognize when a question additionally needs a basic science concept. Review that concept after practice.
strategies.shortcut: Keep a small concept list from missed questions: density, heat, variables, energy and basic biology.
strategies.caution: Not every answer is recoverable from a graph. Guessing the meaning of technical words can mislead you.
strategies.example: Original example: a floating object has lower average density than the fluid it displaces in simple equilibrium.

strategies.title: ACT Writing: plan an argument
strategies.method: Read the issue, perspectives and task. Choose a clear position, supporting reasons and a meaningful relationship to another perspective.
strategies.shortcut: Outline claim → example → explanation before drafting paragraphs.
strategies.caution: A memorized essay that ignores the prompt will not demonstrate analysis. Address the actual competing ideas.
strategies.example: Original example: for a technology policy, explain a concrete benefit, a cost, and why your proposed balance is justified.

strategies.title: ACT Writing: support and revise
strategies.method: Explain how examples support the argument. Reserve part of the session for checking logic, organization and sentence clarity.
strategies.shortcut: Review the thesis and each paragraph’s first sentence to catch a disconnected argument quickly.
strategies.caution: Length alone is not quality. A specific explanation matters more than an invented statistic or ornate vocabulary.
strategies.example: Original example: after describing an outcome, add why it supports your claim and what limitation remains.

strategies.title: Pacing, flags and productive review
strategies.method: When you stop making progress, record a best attempt, flag the question and move on within the current permitted section or module. Return with remaining time.
strategies.shortcut: After practice, separate concept errors from slow correct answers and try a different method on fresh questions.
strategies.caution: Section averages are planning guides, not fixed question deadlines. A shortcut is useful only if accuracy holds on unfamiliar problems.
strategies.example: Original example: compare median time on fresh correct questions before and after a method change; do not count a memorized repeat as new evidence.
